newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai bourse soars as foreigners rush to buy.
newsitem.headline: Thai bourse soars as foreigners rush to buy.

text.p: The Thai stock market continued to soar on Thursday as foreign investors led the rush to buy stocks in a sign of approval of the government's move to float the baht, analysts and traders said.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand's key index was nearly nine percent higher by the midday break, gaining 48.96 points to 617.75. Trade was brisk with about 4.4 billion baht of shares changing hands.
"I think it's a vote of confidence that the Bank of Thailand finally realised we've got a problem," said Graham Catterwell, head of equities for Morgan Grenfell.
"This is amazing," said a foreign analyst. "There has been a lot of panic buying. When people pile in they really want in and don't care. There are still a lot of orders coming in from overseas."
The market, which was mired in eight-year lows for most of the past two months, has gained nearly 90 points in the past two days and moved to levels not seen since early May.

The government's move to float the baht and drop a 13-year old policy of pegging it to a basket of currencies was the latest in a series of measures to help Thailand's economy which has been suffering with high interest rates, low exports and a sharp slowdown in growth.
The baht, which lost about 15-20 percent of its value on Wednesday after the government announced the flotation, was relatively steady from levels late on Wednesday.
The currency was quiet in morning trade, as many investors were still trying to digest and understand the new exchange rate system, which they called a de facto devaluation.
The baht was mostly steady from Wednesday and was quoted around 28.90/29.40 bid/ask offshore and 28.00 in local markets at 0600 GMT.
On Thursday morning the Bank of Thailand set a baht/dollar reference rate, which is a weighted average of the trade on Wednesday, at 27.383.
Analysts said equity investors were not taking much notice of the slight fluctuations in the baht or the reference rate, as many felt most of the drop in the currency's value had already taken place.

"The big hit has already been taken," said one foreign analyst. "But people who are coming in to buy aren't really worried. The market is going up so fast they'll more than recoup any exchange losses."
Somchai Trairattanapirom of SITCA Investment and Securities said he expected to see continued buying interest, especially by foreigners, for the rest of the day.
Traders said there were many bids to buy but few sell offers as most investors thought prices would continue to rise.
